rv.q: Juicy’s spiritual journey takes place at a boisterous Southern backyard barbecue that is funny and fabulous, terrifying and touching.
"Fat Ham" is a total gas — the funniest and most invigorating new show on Broadway.
For me, seeing “Fat Ham,” even multiple times, thus remains a revelation and a balm.
At no point does this play feel like anything other than a big-fun Broadway show: it’s a smart, fearless and often wildly entertaining 90 minutes, filled with radical ideas and absurdist spectacle.
James Ijames has created a brilliant contemporary riff on 'Hamlet' that crackles with wit, wisdom and emotional truth.
By turns sweet and saucy (and very funny), the play stays just close enough to Hamlet to keep us off-balance.
Ali’s direction, Fat Ham is an exhilarating example of Ijames’s world-building, his prowess for merriment and lyrical musing.

James Ijames' Pulitzer Prize-winning play 'Fat Ham' is a raucous, irreverent and ultimately moving riff on 'Hamlet' that brings Shakespeare's tragedy into a contemporary Black family's backyard barbecue.
Ijames' Fat Ham is a reimagining in the most appropriate sense of the word.
With a fresh and vital force, Ijames and Juicy make the Hamlet saga more comedy than tragedy.
Upon exiting the theater, I left with overwhelming admiration for Ijames' ambition, rather than laughing and grooving out of my seat.
Much of Ijames’ “Fat Ham” is playful ideas that don’t add up.

Conceptually, I’m right there with what Ijames is cooking up, but by the time that finale came around, I was left a little cold, craving some pulled pork but, instead, getting a takeout sandwich encased in too many layers of cling wrap.
Without apologies to the purists, it is a modern classic in its own right.
The ensemble is as fabulous as ever.
“Fat Ham” is the most fun you’ll have at any play this Broadway season.
Just be careful you don’t die laughing while watching it.

So it is nothing short of miraculous that James Ijames’s Fat Ham, winner of the 2022. Pulitzer Prize, not only holds up to that comparison, it manages to explore and amplify Shakespeare’s classic and to stand on its own as a wholly original piece of theater.
Ijames has drily noted in the playbill, the setting “could also be Virginia, or Maryland or Tennessee. It is not Mississippi, or Alabama or Florida. That’s a different thing altogether.
Change is possible; we just must want to do it.
Ijames takes Hamlet’s political and social themes and marinates them for a modern audience.
Simply put, for Ijames’ insightfully idiosyncratic take on Hamlet, we’re not in Elsinore anymore, and that’s a good thing.
For Fat Ham is scrumptuously satiating now, meatier and far more meaningful than it was in its off-Broadway incarnation.
You can't help but feel welcome, drawn in, and caught up in the story.
Ijames' characters are as American as pulled pork and baby back ribs, which emphasizes the universality of Shakespeare's work.

As led by an excellent ensemble cast, the solid production (directed by Saheem Ali) successfully balances the play’s intimate emotional moments, terrific stagecraft (including surprise entrances and exits by the ghost) and far-out comedy.

He also delivers what is perhaps the single most memorable moment in “Fat Ham,” a long soliloquy (very much not Shakespearean) about a dream encounter that climaxes in, um, sexual congress with a gingerbread man cookie.
There's a lot to admire in this 95-minute one-act, even if by the end we feel like we've tasted more honey glaze than meat.

Shakespeare is the indisputable dominating figure on stages around the world—delivered in many languages. But, no where does he seem to get more nuanced interpretations than in hometown New York City. This more recent example is a move from Theatre to Broadway in an unconventional spin on the Danish play called “Fat Ham.
It takes that play, messes with it, f**ks it up the ass, and soars.

cn.t: Ijames' Pulitzer-winning Hamlet adaptation wins praise for its audacious, raucous reimagining set at a Black Southern BBQ, with critics applauding its humor and fresh take on masculinity and violence, though some question whether Shakespeare serves the themes.
